clue.text: Apart, in the manner shown below

parts.note: 'as' means in the way or manner of
what is shown below something is under it

explanation.surface: Looks like a note in a manual telling the reader to keep two parts separate, as illustrated in the diagram underneath.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase reads like a cross-reference to a picture below, but read literally, word by word, it spells out an old-fashioned adverb.
explanation.definitionFit: Asunder is a slightly old-fashioned adverb for into separate pieces, as in torn or split into parts.

clue.text: Lead Sindy astray? It could be lust

definitions.note: definition by example: lust is one of the seven

indicators.note: to go astray is to wander off the proper course, so the letters stray out of their order

parts.note: the two words supply the nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone worries that leading the Sindy doll into bad ways might be a matter of lust.
explanation.walkthrough: Sindy is a British fashion doll, a rival to Barbie, which makes the moral panic comic. The definition is an example: lust is one member of a famous set of seven.
explanation.definitionFit: Lust is listed alongside pride, greed, envy, wrath, gluttony and sloth among the seven capital vices of Christian teaching.

clue.text: I will get blasé about this woman

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: 'about' can mean around in a turned-round fashion, so the letters are moved about

parts.note: the five letters, accent dropped, are the material to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone vows to become nonchalant about a particular woman they have been fretting over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning', but it is the instruction to rearrange the word that precedes it; crosswords ignore accents.
explanation.definitionFit: Isabel is a female given name, so a particular woman fits; the clue just needs any girl's name here.

clue.text: Mangled, headless, star rodeo rider found in arena

indicators.note: without a head means the opening letter is taken off
something mangled is crushed out of shape, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: the word with its first letter removed
taken as written

explanation.surface: A celebrity rodeo cowboy has been badly injured, even decapitated, in the arena.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rodeo rider' reads as one phrase, but 'rodeo' belongs to the letters to rearrange and the definition starts at 'rider'.
explanation.definitionFit: Strictly a toreador is a bullfighter, traditionally one on horseback, who performs in the bullring before a crowd.

clue.text: I held on then, with feet broken, as far as you can go

definitions.text: as far as you can go

indicators.note: broken things are smashed into bits that can be reassembled differently

parts.note: eleven letters taken as written
four more letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A walker kept going despite injured feet, reaching the point where they could go no further.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole first phrase plus 'feet' make up fifteen letters, which is a strong hint for a long anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom, from a railway terminus, means the final point beyond which nothing more is possible or permitted.

clue.text: King David's ancestor missing? That's harsh

parts.note: in the Bible Ruth is the great-grandmother of King David
the suffix meaning without, as in hopeless

explanation.surface: Someone protests that leaving out an ancestor of King David from a genealogy is unfair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Missing' looks like it describes the ancestor being absent, but it supplies the suffix for without, joined on after her name.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruthless means pitiless and cruel, without compassion, which matches severe or harsh treatment.

clue.text: Show in Bill, with German following

indicators.note: coming after means this part is placed behind the earlier one

parts.note: a bill is a poster or advertisement, shortened to ad
mit is the German word for with

explanation.surface: A guest called Bill is being shown into a room, accompanied by a German companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name, but it is a notice or advertisement; 'with German' asks for the German for with.
explanation.definitionFit: To admit someone is to let them enter, the same as ushering or showing a visitor inside.

clue.text: Not in company with me? Result!

parts.note: the opposite of in
CO is the abbreviation for company
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is delighted not to be stuck in company with the speaker, crying 'Result!' like a football fan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Result!' is British slang for a lucky win, so the exclamation reads as celebration; here it is simply the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An outcome is the consequence or end product of an event, which is what a result is.

clue.text: Evaluate dullards before beginning of semester

parts.note: asses are stupid people

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A teacher grades the slow students before the new term starts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' just places the dullards ahead of the single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To assess is to judge the quality or value of something, a straightforward synonym of evaluate.

clue.text: Is French friend hosting one judge?

indicators.note: a host takes a guest in, so the outer letters take in another piece

parts.note: est is French for is
the Roman numeral for one
a mate is a friend

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a French friend is putting up a visiting judge.
explanation.walkthrough: The host is the French word and the friend joined together, with the numeral slotted in at their join; 'judge' is a verb here, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: To estimate is to form an approximate opinion of size or value, as when you judge a distance.

clue.text: Dine badly, bile upset: it's not fit to eat!

indicators.note: something done badly is done wrong, so the letters come out in a wrong order

parts.note: four letters to rearrange

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and disturbed, so the letters are tumbled

parts.note: four more letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A diner had a bad meal that turned their stomach and declares the food unfit to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: Each four-letter word is rearranged separately and the two results are joined.
explanation.definitionFit: Inedible describes food that cannot or should not be eaten, because it is spoilt, poisonous or unpalatable.

clue.text: Oil not stirred in moisturiser

indicators.note: stirring mixes things up, so the letters are mixed into a new order

parts.note: six letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A recipe note: the oil in a skin cream should not be stirred in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not stirred' reads as a negative instruction, but 'not' is part of the letters and 'stirred' alone signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A lotion is a thin cream applied to the skin, commonly used to soften or hydrate it.

clue.text: Colour to get bike in that's used again

indicators.note: to get something in is to take it inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: red is a colour
a cycle is a bicycle

explanation.surface: Someone wants to paint a second-hand bicycle so it looks fresh.
explanation.walkthrough: The bike goes inside the colour, between its second and third letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Recycled describes material processed so that it can be put to use once more rather than thrown away.

clue.text: Former pupils better hidden

parts.note: OBs are old boys, ex-pupils of a school
made better, healed

explanation.surface: Alumni who did better than others have been kept out of sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' looks like a comparative adjective but is a past participle: made better, healed. 'Old boys' is the British term for former pupils of a school.
explanation.definitionFit: Something obscured is concealed or blocked from view, so it cannot be seen.

clue.text: Never stopping to entertain British, stiff and formal

indicators.note: entertaining a guest means having them inside your home, so one piece goes within

parts.note: unending means never stopping
B is the abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: A tireless, rigid host keeps on entertaining British visitors in a starchy way.
explanation.walkthrough: The single letter slips in after the first two letters of the word for endless.
explanation.definitionFit: An unbending person is rigid and inflexible in manner, refusing to relax, which is stiff and formal.

clue.text: Hotel in Midlands town becomes industrial unit

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: Worksop is a town in Nottinghamshire, in the English East Midlands
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A hotel in a Midlands town is being converted into an industrial building.
explanation.walkthrough: Worksop is a market town in Nottinghamshire, England; the hotel letter goes inside it near the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A workshop is a room or building where goods are made or repaired, a small factory-type premises.

clue.text: Prolongs sit-ups, on exercising

indicators.note: exercising puts things through their paces, working them into new positions

parts.note: eight letters to rearrange, hyphen and comma ignored

explanation.surface: A gym-goer drags out a session of sit-ups while exercising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exercising' fits the gym picture so well it hides its job as the rearrangement signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To spin something out is to make it last longer than necessary, stretching or drawing it out.

clue.text: Old magazine not down in fight

parts.note: Punch was a long-running British humour magazine, closed in 2002
the opposite of down

explanation.surface: An old magazine is not finished off in a scrap.
explanation.walkthrough: Punch was a famous British satirical weekly; 'punch-up' is British informal for a brawl.
explanation.definitionFit: A punch-up is a fistfight or brawl, an informal word for a physical fight between people.

clue.text: Badge has small heart

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small
ticker is slang for the heart

explanation.surface: A badge has a little heart on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small heart' sounds like a picture on the badge, but it is the size abbreviation plus slang for the heart.
explanation.definitionFit: A sticker is an adhesive label worn or displayed to show support or achievement, as a badge is.

clue.text: Success other eccentric displays up till now

parts.note: a hit is a success

indicators.note: eccentric means off-centre and odd, so the letters are arranged oddly

parts.note: five letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Another odd character has shown success so far.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eccentric' looks like a noun for an oddball, but it is the rearrangement signal applied to 'other'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hitherto is a formal adverb meaning until this point in time, so far or previously.

clue.text: Runner put in also, as salad ingredient

indicators.note: putting something in places it inside, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: too means also
a runner is a long narrow rug or mat

explanation.surface: A runner bean is added to the salad as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runner' suggests the runner bean, a common British vegetable, but it is a strip of carpet.
explanation.definitionFit: Tomatoes are among the most common raw fruits sliced into a mixed green salad.

clue.text: An old frame Charlie's cut for coat

indicators.note: cutting something out removes it, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: taken as written
O is the abbreviation for old
a rack is a framework for holding things
C is Charlie in the NATO phonetic alphabet; it is removed

explanation.surface: An old frame belonging to Charlie has been cut up to make a coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie's cut' means the letter for Charlie is cut from the frame word, not that Charlie did any cutting.
explanation.definitionFit: An anorak is a waterproof hooded jacket, a type of outdoor coat.

clue.text: Learn cooking of kidneys

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so the letters are worked into a new shape

parts.note: five letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An instruction to learn how to cook kidneys.
explanation.walkthrough: The kitchen picture fits the kidneys, but 'cooking' only rearranges the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Renal is the medical adjective relating to the kidneys, from the Latin word for them.

clue.text: Chance to cross a sea for ineffectual person

indicators.note: crossing over something spans it on both sides, so one piece straddles the other

parts.note: luck is chance
taken as written
the Med is short for the Mediterranean Sea

explanation.surface: A hopeless person is told to take a chance on crossing the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The outer word wraps around the inner pair, which sit after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A lame duck is an idiom for someone weak or unsuccessful, unable to cope or achieve anything.

clue.text: Husband to appear twice during saga in odd Asian city

indicators.note: happening during something means within its span, so pieces go inside
odd means strange and irregular, so the letters are put in an irregular order

parts.note: the same letter used a second time
six letters to rearrange
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A husband appears twice in a long story set in a strange city in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd' looks like it describes the city, but it rearranges the two words before it; 'in' is part of those letters, not a link. The two husband letters then slot into the result at separate points.
explanation.definitionFit: Shanghai is China's largest city and a major port, so it is a city in Asia.

clue.text: Note from singer heard?

indicators.note: what is heard is the sound rather than the spelling

parts.note: a tenor is a male singer with a high voice

explanation.surface: Someone asks if a musical note came from a singer they heard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' suggests music, alongside 'singer', but it is a banknote; a tenner is British slang for a ten-pound note.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenner is informal British for a ten-pound banknote, so it is a type of paper money note.

clue.text: Egg's first put into a very soft, whipped pile for this sweet

indicators.note: putting something into another places it inside

parts.note: taken as written
pp, pianissimo, is the musical direction for very soft

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

indicators.note: whipping beats and churns, so the letters are churned into a new order

parts.note: four letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A recipe: put the egg first into a soft whipped mound to make this dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whipped' fits the kitchen scene but rearranges 'pile'; the egg letter goes inside that result, after its first letter. 'Sweet' is British for a dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: Apple pie is a classic baked dessert, and in Britain a dessert course is commonly called a sweet.
